newsitem.title: USA: Einstein's "little calculation" came early in life.
newsitem.headline: Einstein's "little calculation" came early in life.

text.p: Albert Einstein's "little calculation" about a concept called gravitational lensing came much earlier in the life of the famed physicist than previously thought, scientists have discovered.

An article appearing on Friday in the journal Science says Einstein formulated these calculations in 1912 -- three years before he finished his theory of relativity. But he dismissed his own work as too speculative and impossible to prove.

Twenty-four years passed before a Czech electrical engineer and amateur scientist convinced Einstein to publish his notes on the phenonomenon. But even then he described that 1936 article in Science as "of little value" but added of his Czech friend, "it makes the poor guy happy."
The concept was proven in 1979 and is now regarded as an important consequence of the theory of relativity for astrophysics.
The new study of Einstein's early research notes indicates that this theory was completed three years before he completed his theory of relativity.

"These notes show that Einstein had developed the basic theory of gravitational lensing even before he completed the general theory of relativity in 1915," wrote the authors, Jurgen Renn and Tilman Sauer of the Max Planck Institute for the History of Science in Berlin and John Stachel at Boston University.

Gravitational lensing means seeing multiple images of a star if an object is interposed between the star and the observer. The object in the middle has its own gravitational pull that bends light and creates the image.
